newsitem.title: UK: JUDGE TELLS SOCCER BRIBES JURY NOT TO BE STAR-STRUCK.
newsitem.headline: JUDGE TELLS SOCCER BRIBES JURY NOT TO BE STAR-STRUCK.

text.p: The judge in a high-profile English soccer bribes trial told the jury on Thursday not to be overwhelmed by the fame of the stars they had heard giving evidence and the publicity surrounding the case.

"This is a serious trial for soccer because those who play and follow the game expect it not to be corrupted. They expect those who corrupt it to be brought to book," Judge Simon Tuckey told the jury as he started two days of summing up.

The jurors have spent almost seven weeks listening to the case against former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar and ex-Wimbledon keeper Hans Segers, both charged with accepting money to throw matches on behalf of an Asian betting syndicate.
Former Wimbledon and Aston Villa striker John Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim are accused of handing over the money. All four men deny the charges.
"The case has attracted a great deal of publicity. The reason it is so high-profile is because of the allegations and the identity of those against whom they are made," Tuckey said.
"Please don't get carried away and get dazzled by the star quality of those you have heard in court."

Defence lawyers called a number of leading soccer stars and experts -- such as former Liverpool captain Alan Hansen and goalkeeper Gordon Banks, who helped England win the 1966 World Cup -- to testify on behalf of their clients.
The eight men and three women on the jury are expected to start deliberating their decision on Monday. One juror was discharged early in the proceedings.

Tuckey said the jury should treat with caution the evidence given by chief prosecution witness Chris Vincent, who told the court that Grobbelaar, Lim and Fashanu had all been involved in efforts to rig matches.

Vincent was a former business partner of Grobbelaar's but decided to take his story to the Sun newspaper in 1994 after the goalkeeper pulled out of a safari park venture the two men were trying to set up in Zimbabwe.
Vincent, who most of the defence lawyers have portrayed as a treacherous liar, told the court that he wanted to destroy Grobbelaar while making as much money as possible.
"Almost every uncomplimentary adjective in the dictionary has been used to describe him by the defence lawyers," the judge told the jury.
"Vincent's close association with Grobbelaar means you should treat his evidence with caution. His decision to expose Grobbelaar was intended to destroy him, not to expose corruption," he added.
Vincent, who had already been paid 30,000 pounds ($48,800) by the Sun, stood to make significant sums of money from book and film deals if the accused were found guilty, he said.
"These factors clearly give him a motive for lying. There is nothing illegal in what is known as 'kissing and telling', but this doesn't mean he's guilty of lying," Tuckey said.
The judge noted that Segers had lied to police about money he paid into his Swiss bank account and Grobbelaar had lied about money he paid to Vincent.
"In each case you must ask 'Why did he lie?' The mere fact of a lie is not in itself evidence of guilt."

He also said the jury should not necessarily read too much into Fashanu's decision not to give evidence. The star's lawyer said at the time that it was up to the prosecution to prove its case rather than for Fashanu to defend himself. ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
